3sum.d: Find every unique triple of values in the array whose sum is zero. The same triple must not be reported twice.
3sum.i: Sort, fix the first element, then solve two-sum on the rest with two pointers. Skip equal neighbours to avoid duplicate triples instead of using a Set.
k: Sort + fix one + two pointers, skip duplicates
Fix one + HashSet two-sum, dedupe sorted triples in a Set

4sum.d: Return all unique quadruples of values whose sum equals target.
4sum.c: n <= 200, values up to 1e9 (sum can overflow int)
4sum.i: Same idea as 3Sum with one more fixed loop: two nested loops + two pointers. Use long for the sum to avoid overflow.
k: Sort + two fixed indices + two pointers
Three loops + HashSet lookup for the fourth

add-two-numbers.d: Two linked lists hold the digits of two numbers in reverse order (ones digit first). Return their sum as a linked list in the same format.
add-two-numbers.i: Walk both lists together with a carry, treating a finished list as 0. Loop while either list or carry remains; a dummy head simplifies building the result.
k: Single loop with carry and dummy head

alice-and-bob-playing-flower-game.d: Alice picks x in [1,n] flowers for one lane and y in [1,m] for the other; players alternately remove one flower and whoever takes the last one wins. Count pairs (x,y) where Alice (who moves first) wins.
alice-and-bob-playing-flower-game.i: Alice wins exactly when x + y is odd, i.e. one is odd and the other even. Answer = odd(n)*even(m) + even(n)*odd(m) = (n*m)/2.

all-nodes-distance-k-in-binary-tree.d: Given a binary tree, a target node and k, return the values of all nodes exactly k edges away from the target.
all-nodes-distance-k-in-binary-tree.i: A tree is just an undirected graph once you can go upward: record each node's parent, then BFS from the target for k levels with a visited set.
k: Parent map + level BFS from target

amount-of-time-for-binary-tree-to-be-inf.d: An infection starts at the node with value start and spreads to adjacent nodes (children and parent) each minute. Return the minutes until the whole tree is infected.
amount-of-time-for-binary-tree-to-be-inf.i: Same trick as 'distance K': build parent pointers, BFS from start; the answer is the number of BFS levels minus one.

article-views-i.d: From a Views table (article_id, author_id, viewer_id, view_date), list the authors who viewed at least one of their own articles, sorted by id.
article-views-i.ex: rows where author_id = viewer_id -> those author ids
article-views-i.i: Filter author_id = viewer_id, use DISTINCT to remove duplicates, alias the column and ORDER BY.

average-time-of-process-per-machine.d: Each process on a machine has a 'start' and 'end' timestamp row. Report each machine's average processing time (end - start), rounded to 3 decimals.
average-time-of-process-per-machine.i: Self-join the table: one alias for 'start' rows and one for 'end' rows on the same machine+process, then GROUP BY machine and AVG the difference.

balanced-binary-tree.d: Decide whether a binary tree is height-balanced: at every node the heights of the left and right subtrees differ by at most 1.
balanced-binary-tree.i: Compute heights bottom-up (post-order) and check the balance condition in the same pass, so it runs in O(n) instead of O(n^2).
k: Post-order height with a global flag

best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock.d: Given daily prices, choose one day to buy and a later day to sell to maximise profit. Return 0 if no profit is possible.
best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock.i: Scan once, tracking the minimum price seen so far; the best profit when selling today is price - minSoFar.

best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock-ii.d: Same prices array, but you may buy and sell as many times as you like (holding at most one share). Return the maximum profit.
best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock-ii.i: Greedy: every upward step prices[i+1] > prices[i] can be captured, so sum all positive day-to-day differences.

big-countries.d: A country is big if its area is at least 3,000,000 km^2 or its population is at least 25,000,000. Return name, population and area of big countries.
big-countries.ex: Afghanistan: area 652,230 km^2, population 25,500,100 -> big (by population)
big-countries.i: Simple WHERE with OR. (A UNION of two queries can be faster on indexed columns.)

binary-search.d: Search a sorted array of distinct integers for target and return its index, or -1. Must be O(log n).
binary-search.i: Classic template: while (lo <= hi), mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2 avoids overflow; move lo or hi past mid.

binary-tree-inorder-traversal.d: Return the inorder (left, node, right) traversal of a binary tree.
binary-tree-inorder-traversal.i: Iterative version: push all left children onto a stack, pop one, visit it, then move to its right child.

binary-tree-level-order-traversal.d: Return the values of a binary tree level by level, left to right, as a list of lists.
binary-tree-level-order-traversal.i: BFS with a queue; read q.size() at the start of each level so you know how many nodes belong to it.
k: BFS, process one level per iteration

binary-tree-maximum-path-sum.d: A path is any sequence of connected nodes (each used at most once, not necessarily through the root). Return the largest possible path sum.
binary-tree-maximum-path-sum.i: DFS returns the best downward path starting at a node (node + max(0, left, right)); at each node update the global answer with node + max(0,left) + max(0,right), the path that bends there.
k: Post-order DFS with global max, clamp negatives to 0

binary-tree-postorder-traversal.d: Return the postorder (left, right, node) traversal of a binary tree.
binary-tree-postorder-traversal.i: Recursive DFS: visit children first, then the node. Iterative trick: do a modified preorder (node, right, left) and reverse it.

binary-tree-preorder-traversal.d: Return the preorder (node, left, right) traversal of a binary tree.
binary-tree-preorder-traversal.i: Iteratively: pop from a stack, visit, push right child then left child (so left is processed first).
k: Iterative with stack (push right, then left)

binary-tree-right-side-view.d: Looking at a binary tree from the right side, return the values you can see from top to bottom (the last node of each level).
binary-tree-right-side-view.i: Level-order BFS and record the last node of each level. (DFS visiting right first and recording the first node at each new depth also works.)
k: BFS, take last node per level

binary-tree-zigzag-level-order-traversal.d: Level-order traversal, but alternate direction each level: left-to-right, then right-to-left, and so on.
binary-tree-zigzag-level-order-traversal.i: Normal BFS; on odd levels insert each value at the front of the level list (or reverse the list) instead of changing the traversal order.
